channel.title: HAT MI Daily - Macro and Industries
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Indonesia's economy grew 5.47% year on year in the third quarter of 2026, up from 5.29% in the second quarter, with government spending up 8.95%, household consumption up 5.04% and investment up 6.06%, Statistics Indonesia says.
item.description:
Antara News reports that Statistics Indonesia (BPS) says GDP grew 5.47% year on year in the third quarter, up from 5.29% in the second, driven by domestic activity: household consumption rose 5.04%, government spending 8.95% on higher personnel costs and spending on the free nutritious meal programme, and investment 6.06%, helped by the vehicle component, while exports rose 4.59%. A second Antara report quotes the coordinating economics minister Airlangga Hartarto that manufacturing, the largest sector at 19.22% of GDP, grew 5.87% and that household consumption was 51.97% of GDP. MarketScreener says growth was supported by manufacturing, including palm-oil processing for fuel as the mandatory biodiesel programme expanded, and that the state budget assumes growth of 5.4% for 2026 while the finance minister has said it could reach 5.5%. The Jakarta Post gives the same data rounded, 5.5% against 5.3% in the previous quarter. The rows give no figures for construction, no import growth and no regional breakdown.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report headline growth and its demand components, not output by industry beyond manufacturing. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, growth above 5% led by consumption, investment and public spending supports demand for consumer and industrial goods, while the 8.95% rise in government spending depends on budget decisions. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Indonesian manufacturing and vehicle investment are end markets in ASEAN; the rows give no figures for materials or construction. Points that may be worth considering include manufacturing and construction output for the fourth quarter and Bank Indonesia's policy decisions.

Antara News | Antara News | MarketScreener | The Jakarta Post

item.title: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate by a quarter point to 4% on 5 November, its first rise in more than three years, citing volatility in energy markets and the war in the Middle East, and keeps open further rises.
item.description:
The Financial Times reports that Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey announced a quarter-point rise in rates to 4% on 5 November, the first by the Bank for three years, and cited huge volatility in energy markets and the war in the Middle East; it says the Bank is holding the door open to further rises to 4.25% and potentially beyond as inflation moves further from its 2% target. Bloomberg reports Bailey as saying that the longer the Middle East conflict lasts the more inflationary pressure builds in the pipeline, and that the impact of that needs to be limited. The Guardian reports that the rise will immediately lift borrowing costs for the 510,000 homeowners with a base-rate tracker mortgage, and that UK Finance says monthly payments for a typical tracker customer with an outstanding balance of GBP 147,000 will rise by GBP 30.72. Before the decision, the Guardian noted that rates had already risen in 2026 in the US, Japan, the eurozone, Australia and Canada. The rows give no vote split, no inflation figure and no growth forecast.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report the decision and the governor's reasoning, not a path for rates. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a higher Bank Rate raises borrowing costs for households and companies in the United Kingdom and tends to weigh on housing and construction activity with a delay, and the rows tie the decision to energy prices and the war and give no domestic demand data. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, UK construction and manufacturing demand and the sterling cost of imported materials are affected through financing costs and the exchange rate; the rows give no figures for either. Points that may be worth considering include the Bank's next rate decision, UK inflation data and mortgage approvals.

The Financial Times | Bloomberg | The Guardian | The Guardian

item.title: China's commerce ministry says on 5 November that it is open to buying more US farm goods, provided the reciprocal tariff cuts, described as USD 30 billion on each side, are implemented.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that China's Commerce Ministry said on 5 November that China is open to buying US farm goods, but only if the two countries agree on reciprocal tariff cuts; after a September summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in Washington the two sides proposed a package of USD 60 billion of reciprocal cuts, including roughly USD 17 billion of US farm goods that China imported in 2024. The ministry spokesperson, Huang Ling, said that China hopes the US will work with it to create favourable conditions through joint tariff cuts, fewer non-tariff barriers and wider market access. China Daily describes the arrangement as covering around USD 30 billion in imports on each side, and the South China Morning Post and Xhby.net as USD 30 billion on each side. The South China Morning Post adds that the statement followed the Democratic midterm win, which analysts said could complicate trade talks before the APEC summit later in November by raising questions about the Trump administration's ability to honour its commitments. The rows give no tariff rates, no product list beyond farm goods, no date for implementation and no US response.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report China's conditions and analysts' views, not an implemented tariff cut, and the rows differ on whether the package was proposed (MarketScreener) or agreed (South China Morning Post, Xhby.net), and the package is described as USD 60 billion in total (MarketScreener) and USD 30 billion on each side (China Daily, South China Morning Post, Xhby.net); the rows do not say whether both count the same measure. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a conditional offer made before a summit is a negotiating position. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, tariffs between the United States and China affect the cost of chemicals, equipment and finished goods that move between them, so a reciprocal cut limited to farm goods would have little direct effect, while a wider cut would reach industrial inputs; the rows give no product coverage. Points that may be worth considering include the APEC meeting of the two presidents, a published list of covered products and any US statement on the conditions.

MarketScreener | China Daily | South China Morning Post | Xhby.net

item.title: China extends its anti-dumping duties of 254.4% to 267.4% and anti-subsidy duties of 34.2% to 37.7% on US n-propanol for five years from 6 November, after expiry reviews.
item.description:
China Daily reports that the Ministry of Commerce announced on 5 November that anti-dumping duties on n-propanol from the United States will be extended for five years from 6 November 2026; the duties were first imposed in November 2020 for five years, are 254.4% for Dow Chemical and 267.4% for OQ Chemicals and other US exporters, and were kept after a review concluded that dumping could recur or continue if the duties were lifted and could harm Chinese producers. Xinhua reports that the decision followed two expiry reviews, one on the anti-dumping and one on the anti-subsidy measures, and that the anti-subsidy duties, which range from 34.2% to 37.7%, are also extended for five years. Bjd.com.cn reports that the State Council Customs Tariff Commission decided on the countervailing duties on the Ministry of Commerce's recommendation. China Daily names the chemical's uses as food packaging, printing inks and pharmaceuticals. The rows give no import volume or value, no figure for Chinese production or demand, no other source countries and no statement from the US exporters.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report the continuation of existing duties, not a new measure, and give no trade values. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a duty above 250% can make US-origin material unattractive to Chinese buyers, who would then turn to other supply, and a five-year extension fixes that condition into planning. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the rows do not say whether n-propanol is used in adhesive technologies (China Daily names food packaging, printing inks and pharmaceuticals), so any effect on cost and sourcing for producers in China cannot be read from them; the rows give no prices or buyers. Points that may be worth considering include Chinese import data for n-propanol by origin, solvent prices in China and Europe and Chinese trade-defence decisions on other chemicals.

China Daily | Xinhua News | Bjd.com.cn

item.title: Japan's prime minister told France's president on a call of strong concern over the EU's proposed preference for EU-made electric vehicles, and the UK is in talks for British vehicles to count as European.
item.description:
The Mainichi reports that Japan's prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, expressed strong concern in a phone call with France's president, Emmanuel Macron, about the EU's consideration of preferential treatment for electric vehicles made in the bloc under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, and asked France for a proper response. It reports that France and Germany said in a joint statement on 16 October that vehicles made in Japan should not be eligible for the planned incentive framework, and that the deal also excludes electric vehicles made in other non-EU countries such as Türkiye and South Korea, while Britain would be conditionally entitled to preferential treatment. Dünya Gazetesi reports that the EU plan to prioritise European-made products in public purchases and industrial incentives threatens British carmakers and battery makers, that London continues talks with Brussels for British vehicles and parts to count as European under certain conditions, and that no agreement has been reached. ACEA, the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association, and the UK's SMMT published a study by LSE Consulting covering 2014 to 2024, which finds that the EU and the UK remain each other's most important automotive partner, that their value chains have become less integrated and that both rely more on imported inputs. The rows give no draft text of the Act, no rule of origin, no date for the EU decision and no estimate of trade values.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report diplomatic positions and a proposed framework, not an adopted rule. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a local-content preference rewards production inside the bloc and changes where carmakers place plants and which suppliers they qualify, while the exclusion of third countries can lead to counter-measures. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicles and batteries are end markets, so a change in where cars and batteries are built can change which plants and suppliers buy these materials and which formulations are qualified; the rows give no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the text of the proposed Act, the origin rules for UK-made vehicles and parts and any EU agreement with the UK or Japan on treatment.

The Mainichi | Dünya Gazetesi | ACEA

item.title: Airbus reportedly delivered about 74 aircraft in October, bringing deliveries this year to nearly 621, and keeps its target of around 870 for 2026, which would be an all-time record, MarketScreener writes citing Bloomberg.
item.description:
MarketScreener, citing Bloomberg, reports that Airbus delivered around 74 aircraft in October 2026, bringing the number handed over to customers since the start of the year to nearly 621, and that the company maintains its target of around 870 deliveries in 2026, a level that would be an all-time record. To reach it, MarketScreener writes, the group would have to accelerate significantly over the final two months of the year, with continued pressure on its supply chain. The October figure still has to be confirmed when Airbus publishes its commercial statistics. The row gives no split by aircraft family, no order or backlog figures, no figure for October 2025 and no description of the supply-chain constraints.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports an unconfirmed monthly count and a target, not production data. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, deliveries follow production with a delay, and a record target that needs a stronger end of the year points to a need for a faster delivery pace while supply-chain pressure persists. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, aircraft assembly is a possible end market, so production rates at a European aircraft maker can set a demand base for it, while supply-chain bottlenecks can shift when volumes are bought; the row gives no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include Airbus's official October figures, deliveries for November and any change to the target of around 870.

MarketScreener

item.title: At least 38 of 47 local votes tracked by Redbud Consulting favoured data-centre restrictions in the US midterm elections, and Democrats who pledged curbs won governorships in three states, the Financial Times reports.
item.description:
The Financial Times reports that Democrats pledging to restrict data-centre construction won governor elections in three states at the centre of the AI build-out, and that voters favoured restrictions in at least 38 of the 47 local votes tracked by Redbud Consulting; it quotes Michael Cembalest of JPMorgan Asset Management that about 37 gigawatts of data centres due in 2028 may face an outright pause. The Boston Globe reports that local referendums in places including Wells, Maine, Defiance, Ohio, and Emporia, Kansas, approved bans or restrictions, that the Senate candidates Jon Husted in Ohio and Ken Paxton in Texas, both backed by big tech, lost, and that the analyst Dan Ives sees a big hurdle for the build-out, particularly in Texas. USA Today reports that Texas's newly elected governor, Gina Hinojosa, said on 5 November that Texas is done with data centres unless the companies prove they will benefit Texans; it gives, from the tracking group Cleanview, more than 80 centres operating in Texas, 50 under construction and more than 120 planned. MarketScreener quotes Partners Group that Texas, Georgia and Ohio elected governors or state officials who campaigned on restrictions and together hold about 37%, roughly 100 gigawatts, of the announced US pipeline through 2030, and that the results are more likely to change where and how centres are built than whether. Commercial Times quotes SemiAnalysis that 2027 capacity is unlikely to be affected in the short term because most projects are under construction, while more than 90% of the 62.2 gigawatts planned for 2028 has not started. The rows give no enacted state law or moratorium and do not say whether the local bans voters approved have taken effect, no start date for any restriction and no cancelled project.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report votes, statements and analyst estimates, not an enacted state restriction, and the estimates of exposed capacity differ by source. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, data centres are large construction projects, so restrictions in states with large pipelines would first affect projects that have not started, which matches SemiAnalysis's split between 2027 and 2028 capacity. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, large non-residential construction and the manufacturing of data-centre equipment are possible end markets, so a slower build-out could reduce the volume sold into that segment, while a move to other states would change where it is sold; the rows give no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include new state or local moratoria, project cancellations in Texas and later capacity updates from analysts.

The Financial Times | The Boston Globe | USA Today | MarketScreener | Commercial Times

item.title: German industrial orders rose 4.4% month on month in September after a revised 10.1% fall in August, below the 4.8% analysts expected, the Federal Statistical Office says.
item.description:
The Federal Statistical Office reported on 5 November that orders in German manufacturing rose 4.4% in September on the previous month, seasonally and calendar adjusted, after a fall of 10.1% in August that was revised from a first estimate of 10.6%. Wallstreet:online and MarketScreener give a 10.5% rise in automotive orders as the main driver and MarketScreener and Commercial Times add 8.3% growth in orders for machinery and equipment, while Commercial Times and Chinatimes.com attribute the 10.5% to manufacturing orders as a whole, which the 4.4% total in the same rows rules out. MarketScreener says analysts had expected a rise of 4.8%, and Commercial Times names Reuters as the source of that forecast. Commercial Times says part of the monthly rise reflects a low base after two months in which production changes and factory holidays held orders down, and that orders in the third quarter were 0.2% above the second quarter; Wallstreet:online says orders for other vehicle manufacturing, which includes military vehicles, fell again. MarketScreener adds that the VDMA says orders in mechanical and plant engineering rose 14% in real terms on the year in September, largely against an unusually weak comparison, and sees the upswing as tenuous. The rows give no split between domestic and foreign orders, no index level and no all-industry comparison with September 2025.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report one month of orders after a steep fall, and the VDMA's caution is part of the reporting. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, orders lead production by some months, so a one-month recovery after a 10.1% fall says less about demand than the small 0.2% rise of the third quarter over the second. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, German orders for cars and machinery can set the volume that adhesive technologies can sell into assembly lines with a delay; the rows give no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the orders data for October, German industrial production for September and the split of car and machinery orders between domestic and foreign customers.

Wallstreet:online | MarketScreener | Commercial Times | Chinatimes.com

item.title: The VDA reports that 326,300 passenger cars were produced in Germany in October, down 7% year on year, and exports of 246,500 units were down almost 10%.
item.description:
The Association of the German Automotive Industry (VDA) reports that German plants produced 326,300 passenger cars in October 2026, 7% fewer than a year earlier, and that exports in October were 246,500 units, almost 10% fewer than in the same month of last year. For January to October it reports production of 3.37 million cars, down 4% on the previous year, and exports of 2.54 million units, down 5%. The row gives no breakdown by drive type, brand or destination, no domestic order figure and no reason for the October decline.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports production and exports of passenger cars for one month and the year to date, not sales or registrations. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a fall in German car output reduces the volume of materials that car plants buy, and the 4% decline for the year to date is consistent with October being part of a longer trend, since the year-to-date figure includes October. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, car output volumes can set a base for demand from carmakers and their suppliers, while the mix of vehicle types changes which materials are specified; the row gives no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the VDA's November production figures, exports by destination and output announcements by German carmakers.

VDA

item.title: Brent crude rose about 3.8% to USD 98.20 a barrel on 5 November after an 8.7% fall on 4 November, while crude exports from four Gulf producers in October were 15 million barrels a day, against about 20 million before the war.
item.description:
Anadolu Agency reports that Brent crude rose about 3.8% to USD 98.20 a barrel on 5 November and European natural gas about 2.4% to EUR 90.2 per megawatt-hour, recovering part of the losses that followed the Democratic midterm win and hopes of a diplomatic end to the US–Iran war; it says Qatar is mediating between Washington and Tehran and that forecasts of colder weather in north-western Europe were expected to lift heating demand. Commercial Times gives the preceding move: Brent fell 8.7% on 4 November to USD 94.62 and West Texas Intermediate closed at USD 88.12, both the lowest since 31 August, after Brent had approached USD 118 on 30 October; it adds that US crude inventories fell by 865,000 barrels and that Vortexa data show oil product exports from the Persian Gulf region at 17.1 million barrels a day in October, about three-quarters of the pre-war level. WirtschaftsWoche, citing tanker data, reports that crude exports from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Kuwait were 15 million barrels a day in October, up 10% (the row gives no base period), against about 20 million before the war, and that Brent remains far from its pre-war level of just over USD 60. These are different measures: product exports of a region and crude exports of four countries. The Economic Times reports that spot premiums for Middle East crude have returned to pre-war levels, with Dubai's cash premium to swaps falling to 65 US cents a barrel before recovering slightly, and that Murban exports reached a record 2.4 million barrels a day in September. The Globe and Mail reports BofA Securities' view that 2026 supply disruptions are the largest in data going back to 1965. The rows give no official US or Iranian text on talks (Commercial Times only relays the Iranian president's remark on peace talks and Trump's remark that there were no immediate plans to attack Iran), no shipping count for the Strait of Hormuz and no prices for resins, solvents or freight.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report prices, exports and premiums, not a change in the cost of materials. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a rebound of 3.8% the day after an 8.7% fall suggests, as Commercial Times describes, that the lower level rested on expectations of a deal, and the rows point both to more Gulf supply (higher exports, premiums at pre-war levels) and to a remaining gap (inventories down, product exports at about three-quarters of the pre-war level). On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, crude and gas prices feed into the cost of resins, solvents and energy-intensive intermediates with a delay, so a price that moves several percent a day makes input costs harder to plan; the rows give no prices for these materials. Points that may be worth considering include Brent and European gas prices over the coming trading days, the outcome of the Qatar-mediated contacts and Gulf export data for November.

Anadolu Agency | Commercial Times | WirtschaftsWoche | The Economic Times | The Globe and Mail

item.title: Lanxess's chief executive calls the situation the toughest crisis he has seen for German export industry and expects more consolidation, as Lanxess cuts 550 jobs and lowers the top of its profit forecast to EUR 500 million.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that Lanxess chief executive Matthias Zachert expects further consolidation in the chemical sector and sees BASF's bid for Evonik as a logical consequence of the difficult market, aimed at synergies and economies of scale. He called the situation the toughest crisis for the export-oriented German industry that he has experienced in his professional career. For Lanxess the priority is stabilising the company, which includes a cost-cutting programme and the elimination of 550 jobs worldwide. The company lowered the upper end of its annual forecast for adjusted operating profit (EBITDA) to a range of EUR 450 million to EUR 500 million, from a previous upper end of EUR 550 million. In the third quarter, adjusted profit was EUR 139 million, up 11.2% (the row gives no comparison period), and the net loss narrowed to EUR 70 million from EUR 77 million a year earlier. The row gives no details of the BASF bid, no demand or price data for Lanxess's products, no regional split of the 550 jobs and no statement from BASF or Evonik.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports one company's results and its chief executive's view, not a measure of the whole industry. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, an expectation of more takeovers is a view of how companies may respond to a weak market, not a decided transaction, and job cuts and a lowered forecast at a large chemical producer point to weak demand or high costs in its markets. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, consolidation among chemical producers can change who supplies raw materials and intermediates and on what terms, and a weak market for producers can affect supplier availability and pricing; the row gives no figures for adhesive raw materials. Points that may be worth considering include further quarterly results of European chemical producers, offer documents in the BASF and Evonik case and announcements of capacity closures.

MarketScreener
